author: Josh Hoggard
title: Victims testify in trial of alleged serial rapist at MSU - NewsBreak
text:
By Josh Hoggard ,
2 hours ago
AUTHOR’S NOTE: This story contains details from court documents that include allegations of sexual abuse. Due to the content of this story, discretion is advised before reading. If you know or suspect that a person is being physically or sexually abused, you can submit an anonymous report on the Texas Abuse Hotline Website . If the situation is urgent, please call 1-800-252-5400 .
WICHITA FALLS ( KFDX/KJTL ) — All three alleged victims took the witness stand on the first day of the trial of a former Midwestern State University football player accused of a series of sexual assaults on the college campus.
Haeven Watson in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) Haeven Givon Watson, 21, of Converse, Texas , stands accused of four counts of aggravated sexual assault and one count of burglary of a habitation, intending to commit a sexual offense. He’s been in custody since Dec. 23, 2024, on bonds totaling over $1 million.
After a jury pool of 88 residents of Wichita County was narrowed down to ten men and two women on Tuesday, July 14, 2026, testimony began in Watson’s trial on Wednesday, July 15, in the 78th District Court, with Judge Meredith Kennedy presiding.
PREVIOUS STORY: Jury sworn in for trial of alleged MSU serial rapist John Gillespie, Wichita County District Attorney, is prosecuting the case with assistance from Chelsea Carlton, Assistant District Attorney. Bob Estrada, a long-time defense attorney from Texoma, is representing Watson with the assistance of fellow defense attorney Holly Crampton.
Opening statements from prosecution Proceedings began at around 9 a.m. on Wednesday, July 15, with Judge Kennedy reading the indictment in open court. Watson pleaded not guilty to each of the five counts pending against him.
Gillespie then presented an opening statement to the jury, outlining the case that prosecutors intend to present during Watson’s trial from three alleged incidents between Sept. 24 and Oct. 11, 2024, on the campus of MSU.
John Gillespie in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) During his opening statement, Gillespie described that the first alleged incident occurred on Sept. 24, 2024, and is charged as count 4 of the indictment. The second incident occurred on Oct. 3, 2024, and is charged as the first three counts of the indictment.
Gillespie explained that the final count of the indictment, burglary of a habitation, intending to commit a sexual offense, occurred on Oct. 11, 2024. He explained that each of the incidents involved a different female victim.
“At the conclusion of this case, I think you will find the evidence shows beyond a reasonable doubt that this defendant is guilty of all counts, and I ask that you find him guilty,” Gillespie said.
Estrada chose to exercise his right to preserve his opening statement for the beginning of the defense’s case in chief.
WFPD Sergeant takes the stand first The first witness called on the prosecution’s behalf was Sgt. Marissa Hughes with the Crimes Against Persons Unit of the Wichita Falls Police Department.
Sgt. Hughes testified that the WFPD was called by the MSU Police Department to assist with an investigation into two reports of sexual assaults that had occurred at the Sundance Court Apartments on the campus of MSU on Sept. 24 and Oct. 3, 2024.
“My level of concern was major,” Sgt. Hughes testified. “I believe that any time you have an offense like that, especially at a college campus, it’s concerning.”
Det. Marissa Hughes in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) Sgt. Hughes added that at the time, she had a daughter who was attending MSU, which elevated her level of concern. She testified that a serial rapist is a threat to public safety.
Sgt. Hughes then testified that she believed the two assaults were connected because the suspect in each had a very similar modus operandi, including:
Victims waking up and finding a suspect in their room Same description of appearance and clothing Proximity of the two apartments Both doors were unlocked at the time of the assaults AUTHOR’S NOTE: In an effort to protect the identities of the three alleged victims, they will be identified throughout coverage of Watson’s trial by pseudonyms:
Victim 1 — “Jane” — Aggravated sexual assault — September 24, 2024 Victim 2 — “Kylie” — Aggravated sexual assault (x3) — October 3, 2024 Victim 3 — “Sarah” — Burglary of a habitation with intent to commit a sex offense — October 11, 2024 First alleged victim testifies in Watson’s trial Carlton then called the first alleged victim, who will be referred to as “Jane”, to the witness stand. She testified that she and a friend had been hanging out in her apartment at Sundance Court on Sept. 23, 2024, until about 1 a.m. on Sept. 24, 2024. She testified she fell asleep with her phone by her head at around 1:45 a.m.
“Jane” then testified that she first woke up because she heard something, so she turned around and saw a figure kneeling on her bed, wearing all black except for a white bandana on their face. She testified she was led to believe that the suspect had a gun and that he threatened to kill her.
Haeven Watson in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) “I was freaking out and half asleep,” the first victim testified. “It’s like nothing I’ve ever experienced. Who’s this stranger that’s saying they’re going to kill me?”
“Jane” testified that she felt as if her life was in someone else’s hands, so she needed “to do anything to not die.” She then recalled in graphic detail the alleged assault.
At multiple times while “Jane” was testifying, Estrada objected on the grounds of a narrative that the witness appeared to be establishing. Judge Kennedy overruled the objection, allowing the witness to continue testifying each time.
“Jane” testified that while the suspect was assaulting her, he said, “That’s what you get for making fun of me in class.” She testified that she replied, “Dude, I don’t know you.” She testified that before he left, the suspect said, “If you tell anybody about this, I’m going to kill you. Keep your head down until I leave.”
“Jane” testified that once the suspect left, she wanted to call the police, but she was unable to find her phone. She testified that she eventually found it in her freezer, and that since she knew she fell asleep with her phone next to her, she knew the suspect had placed her phone in the freezer.
Chelsea Carlton in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) “Jane” testified that after she called 911, she spoke to an officer at the scene and was taken to United Regional for a SANE exam. She testified that she’d left her apartment door unlocked because she had a habit of locking herself out, and it cost money each time someone had to come let her back in.
“Jane” testified that she had never met Watson.
PREVIOUS STORY: MSU student accused of burglaries also charged with sexual assault On cross-examination, “Jane” testified that she never saw the suspect’s face and that she could not confirm the identity of the person who raped her. She also testified that she couldn’t clearly remember whether or not she saw a gun during the alleged assault.
SANE nurse recalls exam of first victim Gillespie then called Katelyn Bashford, a registered nurse and Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner at United Regional. She testified that she conducted the SANE exam on “Jane”, explaining the methodology to the jury.
Bashford then read her report, including the statement made by “Jane” during the SANE exam, which was similar to the testimony given by “Jane”. She testified that during her statement, “Jane” said she’d told the suspect, “You have the wrong person.”
Katelyn Bashford in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) On cross-examination from Estrada, Bashford testified that she didn’t note any bodily injuries during the SANE exam, adding that there were no signs that choking or strangulation had occurred.
Bashford testified on cross-examination that a SANE exam cannot determine whether or not a person was sexually assaulted, and that the statement taken during a SANE exam is based on the recollection of the person being examined.
Second alleged victim takes the stand After the jury returned to the courtroom at around 1:30 p.m. following a lunch break, Gillespie called the second alleged victim, who will be referred to as “Kylie”. She testified that on Oct. 2, 2024, she’d gone to sleep and wasn’t wearing her hearing aids.
“Kylie” testified that she woke up to a guy pointing a gun at her head. She testified that she didn’t know what was going on at first, so she swatted at the gun a few times before the suspect eventually pressed it against her forehead.
Haeven Watson in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) “He was wearing a grey zip-up hoodie, and the bottom half of his face… He had a purple bandana on,” the second victim testified. “The only thing I could see about his face was his eyes and his forehead.”
“Kylie” testified that she realized the gravity of “what was about to happen” and was scared for her life because the suspect had a gun. She then recalled the alleged assaults in graphic detail. She testified that she felt “disgusting” while the assault was taking place.
“Kylie” testified that once the suspect left her apartment, she called her boyfriend at the time and told him, “I was just raped.” She testified that she later called the MSU police and spoke with an officer before going to United Regional for a SANE exam.
On cross-examination, “Kylie” testified that she’d never met or seen Watson before the assault or since it took place, but added she never saw the suspect who assaulted her. She testified that she was never shown a photo lineup.
Third alleged victim testifies John Gillespie in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) On Thursday afternoon, at around 3:00 p.m., Gillespie called the third alleged victim, who will be referred to as “Sarah.” She testified that on Oct. 11, 2024, she was living in a dorm in the McCullough-Trigg residence hall on the campus of MSU.
“Sarah” testified that she’d been notified by a campus alert of a possible rapist on campus. She testified that it was concerning to her.
“Sarah” testified that on Oct. 11, 2024, she was on her bed in her room. She stated that sometime in the morning, before noon, a person entered her apartment and grabbed her by both shoulders. She testified that the suspect had dreadlocks, was wearing red sweatpants and a black shirt, as well as a bandana on his face.
“Sarah” testified that when the suspect grabbed her, there was a struggle. She testified that she screamed, and the suspect attempted to “shush” her. She testified that she continued screaming, and the suspect let her go and walked out of her apartment fast.
Haeven Watson in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) “Sarah” testified that due to the recent assaults that had occurred in Sundance Court, she immediately thought that when the suspect had entered her apartment, that was probably what was about to happen.
On cross-examination, “Sarah” testified that she was notified of the two assaults at Sundance by an e-mail alert. She testified she wasn’t able to remember what the alert said. She also testified that she never identified the suspect as Watson, and that the suspect didn’t say anything of a sexual nature to her.
MSU housing director concludes first day PREVIOUS STORY: MSU student disturbed after burglar enters dorm The final witness called to the stand by the prosecution on the first day of testimony in Watson’s trial was Kristi Schulte, Director of Housing at MSU. She testified that she’s been in the role for 10 years.
John Gillespie speaking with Kristi Schulte in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) Schulte testified that in the fall of 2024, she began an effort to communicate to students living on campus tips on safety after two sexual assaults had been reported at Sundance Court. She testified that there was concern from residents across campus at the time.
Schulte testified that at the time, cameras were only at the entrances of the Sundance Court building, and Watson lived on the first floor of Sundance, so he would’ve had key card access to the apartment, and he wouldn’t have been seen entering or leaving on the security footage.
Schulte testified that when she heard about the burglary at McCullough-Trigg on Oct. 11, 2024, she recognized similarities between the description of the suspect and the suspects involved in the two assaults at Sundance.
Schulte testified that one of her colleagues was able to recover security footage from McCullough-Trigg from Oct. 11. Still images from that footage were shown in open court, depicting a person who appeared to be Watson leaving the building.
Surveillance photo of Haeven Watson shown in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) Prosecutors are set to call more witnesses when testimony resumes in the 78th District Court on Thursday, July 16, 2026. Proceedings are expected to begin at around 9 a.m.
This is a developing story. Stick with Texoma’s Homepage for updates as more information becomes available. All individuals charged with a crime are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Haeven Watson in the 78th District Court on Wednesday, July 15, 2026 (Photo credit: Josh Hoggard, KFDX/KJTL) “I was freaking out and half asleep,” the first victim testified.
